paper.title: The labor market gender gap in Denmark: Sorting out the past 30 years
paper.journal: Labour Economics 56 (2019) 58-67 (running head on every page); received 22 May 2017, accepted 26 November 2018, available online 6 December 2018. The PDF's own metadata gives the issue year as 2018.
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement is printed. The paper states only that “The data source for this paper is Danish administrative data primarily from the database IDA” and that Statistics Denmark constructs the hourly wage measure and …

registers.role: sample frame; treatment (gender, parenthood); outcomes (hourly wages, hours worked, yearly earnings, weeks worked, employment); controls (age, experience, occupation, industry); linkage to establishments and firms
variables_mentioned: industry (five-digit classification based on NACE rev. 2)
occupation (ISCO88 after 1990; primary labor market attachment before 1991)
accumulated labor market experience (total registered working hours based on mandatory pension payments)

registers.name_in_paper: Statistics Denmark's hourly wage measure, based on hours worked as estimated from mandatory pension contributions, with an accompanying wage and uncertainty flag
registers.role: outcomes (hourly wages and hours worked); quality screen on the sample

registers.name_in_paper: education data based on a four-digit educational classification (the variable defined as hﬀsp by Statistics Denmark)
registers.role: controls and decomposition component (education); segregation by education track

registers.name_in_paper: background information on the birthdates of children
firm accounting data on value added per worker
registers.role: normalisation of the by-gender AKM establishment effects in the appendix subsample; not available back to 1980
variables_mentioned: employment-weighted average value added per worker at establishment J

linkages: Labor market outcomes for employed individuals, and identifiers for both the establishment and the firm (from 1995), are linked to the individual from 1980 onwards using unique establishment and firm identifiers
Establishments and firms are connected to workers in the last week of November of every year
Industry, occupation and municipality of work are linked to establishment and individual identifiers
Background information on education, gender and the birthdates of children is added to the individual records to form the primary sample
For the AKM decompositions, workers and establishments are linked into the largest connected set of workers and establishments within each decade

sample.universe: Men and women between 25 and 60 years old in Denmark, 1980 to 2010
selection_rules: restrict to men and women between 25 and 60 years old in all years
include only workers who report positive total earnings
include only positive, high quality wages (not heavily imputed from bracketed hours worked); this drops between 12 and 19 percent of observations with positive earnings
include only workers with positive days worked per year
working at least half time (at least half of 37 hours per week)
for the Blinder-Oaxaca decompositions (Tables 2 and 4): additionally restrict to occupation and education groups with at least 50 individuals of each gender
for the AKM decompositions (Tables 3 and 5): exclude those not working in the largest connected set of workers and establishments, estimated separately for 1980-1989, 1990-1999 and 2000-2009
for the parenthood regressions (Table 6): restrict to women and men aged 25-45, because older workers generally have older children no longer in the home
for the education segregation figures (Figs. 2 and 3): all Danes between 25 and 60, not only half-time-plus workers
for the part-time figure (Fig. 6) and footnote 4: the entire population of employed workers

construction_notes: Earnings and wages are deflated according to the Danish 2012 consumer price index

Hourly wages are created by Statistics Denmark from hours worked estimated from mandatory pension contributions; the hours are bracketed (for example 0-8 hours per week is one bracket), so wage estimates are extremely noisy for workers working few hours and Statistics Denmark attaches an uncertainty flag; the paper uses only high-quality (non-flagged) wage observations
All full-time workers fall into the same hours bracket, which the paper names as a pitfall of the data
Accumulated labor market experience is measured as the sum of total hours worked over the lifetime (total registered working hours based on mandatory pension payments)

Education is measured as dummies capturing the interaction of broad major (humanities, social science, etc.) with level of education (technical school, college degree, masters, etc.), at the four-digit level

Occupation is the ISCO88 three-digit classification after 1990 and a measure of primary labor market attachment (constructed by Statistics Denmark on ILO recommendations) before 1991; in the 1980 decompositions occupation categories are blue collar, white collar, high-skilled and management
Industry is a five-digit classification based on NACE rev. 2; the decompositions use two-digit industry code indicators
Weeks worked excludes time when parents are on parental leave as well as unemployment spells
Part time is defined as working less than full time, i.e. less than 37 hours per week; the main samples require at least half time (at least half of 37 hours per week)
Firm is measured as the establishment (physical address) where a worker is employed; establishment ID is available since 1980 and consistent over time, while firm ID starts in 1995

The Duncan and Duncan (1955) index of dissimilarity, Eq. (1), is computed by year for establishments, three-digit ISCO occupations, and four-digit education groups split into less-than-college and college-and-above

links.pointer_quote: While differences in worker characteristics (experience, education, occupation, and industry) explained more than half of the 30-log point gender wage gap in 1980, differences in these characteristics explain only about one third of the twenty log-point gender wage gap in 2010.

claims.statement: In 1980, the raw (unadjusted) gap in the Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition of the gender wage gap (male minus female log hourly wage) is 0.300 log points.

register_source.value: IDA (demographic information on the Danish population, such as gender and age)

definition.value: Sex as recorded in the register. The decomposition reports the male-minus-female difference, so a positive value means the average for men exceeds the average for women.

timing.value: measured in the same cross-section year (1980) as the outcome

register_source.value: IDA (hourly wage measure created by Statistics Denmark from hours worked estimated from mandatory pension contributions); register variable name not given

definition.value: Log hourly wage. Statistics Denmark creates a measure of hourly wages based on hours worked as estimated from mandatory pension contributions; only high-quality (non-flagged) wage observations are used, and wages are deflated by the Danish 2012 consumer price index. The table reports the average over men and over women.

timing.value: cross-section in the calendar year of the column (1980)

units.value: log points of the male-minus-female difference in log hourly wage

magnitude.interpretation: the introduction calls this “the 30-log point gender wage gap in 1980”

estimand.target_population: Danish men and women aged 25-60 working at least half time and not in school, in 1980

population.description: All 25-60 year olds in Denmark working at least half time (at least half of 37 hours per week), not in school, with positive total earnings, positive high-quality hourly wages and positive days worked per year, in 1980
population.selection: conditioned on half-time-plus employment with a high-quality (non-imputed) wage observation, positive earnings and positive days worked, and on not being enrolled in school; occupation and education groups with fewer than 50 individuals of each gender are dropped

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional differences between men and women within a single calendar year; no exogenous variation is used. Separate log wage regressions by gender, with male-female differences in characteristics evaluated at the female coefficients.

key_assumptions.assumption: The decomposition is descriptive: each component measures how much of the raw male-female gap gender differences in that characteristic would predict, not the causal effect of the characteristic.
Gender differences in characteristics are valued at the coefficients of the female log wage regression.
key_assumptions.supported_by: stated in the note to Table 2 and in the text describing the method

key_assumptions.assumption: Discrimination does not contaminate the estimated role of observables; the authors state that it may, and that their estimates would then overstate the role of falling segregation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: footnote 7 argues that if discrimination had fallen the unexplained portion of the gap should have fallen, which it has not in Denmark

implies_edges.from: discrimination (unobserved)

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on working at least half time with positive total earnings, positive days worked and a high-quality wage observation, and on not being in school; the decomposition additionally drops occupation and education groups with fewer than 50 individuals of each gender.
key_assumptions.supported_by: sample selection section and footnote 6

implies_edges.from: selection into the half-time-plus, high-quality-wage sample

threats_discussed: discrimination may contaminate estimates of the role of observables (footnote 7)
occupation and education groups with fewer than 50 individuals of each gender are dropped, so sample sizes differ from Table 1 (footnote 6)
low-quality (heavily imputed) wage observations are dropped, which removes 12 to 19 percent of observations with positive earnings
robustness_checks: the decomposition is repeated in three separate cross-sections (1980, 1995, 2010)
Fig. 4 repeats the decomposition for all workers, workers under 35, non-parents and parents
unresolved_confounders: discrimination may contaminate the estimated role of observables: the coefficients from the female regressions may be “too small” because of discrimination, in which case the estimates overstate the role of falling segregation

estimator.value: Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition: separate OLS log wage regressions for men and women, with male-female differences in observables evaluated at the female coefficients

estimation.specification: Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition of log wages in 1980, 1995 and 2010 into experience (linear, squared, cubic), two-digit industry indicators, four-digit education indicators, occupation indicators and age indicators; no estimating equation is printed for the decomposition.
controls: experience, experience squared and experience cubed
three-digit ISCO occupation indicators (1995 and 2010); blue collar, white collar, high-skilled and management (1980)

heterogeneity.finding: the same decomposition is reported for 1980, 1995 and 2010; this claim is the 1980 column

“in general fathers and mothers have the largest diﬀerences in these characteristics. For non-parents, none of the diﬀerence in male-female wages can be attributed to the sum of diﬀerences in sorting on education, ﬁrm, and occupation in 2010”
